  and pattern vocabulary; both final rounds returned only already-read pages, and the snapshot was
  4445fa068e7a0392182bb996f9e6c6dcd4dc0bdb6dd991fec215d020f2f8e04a.
core_claims: The four input statuses are measured, assumed, derived and unknown; unknown means no defensible value exists and the model must not invent one, and the dual-write lag input is assumed with the missing item recorded as a measured lag distribution.

Substituting zero is an assumption, not a neutral placeholder, and it changes the model: the verified test for zero lag passing with no divergence means a zero-lag run removes the divergence mechanism and answers a different model.

That run still emits precise metrics - success rate 1.0, a finite divergence interval and a rollback completion fraction - so the result is precise but meaningless, the recorded 'unknown as zero' failure mode, and it is not evidence about a real migration.

A model can be verified, converged and executable and still fail to support a decision, because the missing evidence is about the world rather than the code; the defensible outcome is therefore insufficient evidence, not a forced recommendation.

The insufficient-evidence record must name the missing measurement, the range that would support or reject the decision, the owner of the measurement, the consequence of staying in the current state and the next review trigger.

A hard input that is assumed and whose range spans the decision boundary is an explicit insufficient-evidence condition, and repeating an assumed value in a decision record does not make it measured; only new evidence changes a parameter's status.
optional_claims: A sensitivity ranking is not evidence and must not be used to fill a missing measurement.

JCGM 100 supplies measurement and uncertainty vocabulary, but V12 does not perform a metrological uncertainty budget, and a confidence interval across replications is a sampling interval rather than a coverage interval for the inputs.

The modernization record's actionable remedy is a measured dual-write lag distribution, measured reconciliation throughput under target load, a rehearsed rollback and a measured divergence below the business threshold.

tasks.question: A zero-server boundary case runs to completion without raising an error and is recorded as pass. Why is that record not a verification result, and what must distinguish a boundary test from a smoke test?

# Q249 — A zero-server boundary case recorded as pass

**Layer.** Primary: modeling-and-simulation (V12 model verification, contracts and validation limits). Supporting: book (V06's smoke-test caveat; the operations liveness/readiness pattern). The core evidence is V12 because the question is about what counts as a model-verification result.

**Search saturation.** Each facet was searched with two to four formulations in the modeling layer, plus book and atlas checks for "smoke", "boundary test" and "verification case". The final rounds returned the same V12 pages and no new section keys, so I stopped. The V12 pages I read do not define "smoke test"; that definition is marked as inference below.

## 1. Direct answer

The record is not a verification result because it records an execution event — the engine returned without raising — and not the boundary outcome the case exists to verify. A V12 verification case is a record with an identifier, a description, an expected result, an observed result, a pass/fail/not-run status and a test path. A case marked pass without an observed result is a claim, not evidence; a case without a test path is not a verification case. "The test checks that the function returns, not that the result is correct" is a named failure mode, and a strict schema that accepts the fields cannot detect a false claim.

A boundary test must assert the boundary outcome — for zero servers, no service: zero completions, requests rejected or held in backlog according to the model, conservation and non-negativity, no division-by-zero artifact — and it must be able to fail when that outcome is wrong. A smoke test only shows that the path starts and returns; it has no boundary oracle and no power to detect a wrong boundary result. It is a liveness/wiring check, useful as a precondition, not as verification.

## 2. Facet matrix (six facets)

Legend: MC = tycho.page.4e13fd6ac1103a15c800e939b13bd2f9; MV = tycho.page.621e495fcadc4849d2f21d55be4c52e4; MS = tycho.page.d8d9d15b402d8f65928ca0e3f3e5b939; RP = tycho.page.201248045fa3cd67e617ce04a1c56feb; RE = tycho.page.687d2196433c3b076d00c73144dad431; Q = tycho.page.c264e48a38af3148eff0c87a3b98a8dd; V06 = tycho.page.a4335241afc0408d9e137bc2a027ebed; H = tycho.page.43c706143e9208cbcb1770bcc62e9695; CAL = tycho.page.b0c704c825b2faf15a1d118dc9a6b1cc.

| Facet | Query formulations used | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| F1. What makes a pass a verification result | "run record status pass observed result"; "pass without observed result claim"; "verification theater"; "reference case record identifier pass fail not-run" | MC#a-reference-case-record; MS#required-structure; MS#failure-modes |
| F2. Execution success vs. behavioral correctness | "run completes without error pass"; "test asserts outcome not completion"; "falsifiable test assertion fails"; "test can never fail moving target" | MC#failure-modes; MV#conservation; RE#a-run-s-life-cycle |
| F3. Zero-server boundary semantics and oracle | "zero servers boundary case"; "zero servers no service"; "servers"; "queue capacity backlog rejection" | MV#boundary-cases; MC#case-3-boundary-cases; Q#the-basic-quantities; Q#backpressure |
| F4. Boundary test vs. smoke test | "smoke test boundary test"; "smoke test"; "smoke check liveness"; "deployment smoke check" | MC#failure-modes; V06#6-a-reproducible-evaluation-design; H#overview |
| F5. Verification scope and validity limits | "validation status model-verified"; "model-verified production-verified"; "what is not verified"; "boundary case validation" | MV#verification-versus-validation; MV#what-is-not-verified; MC#overview; CAL#overview |
| F6. Evidence-integrity failure modes | "verification theater"; "testing happy path only"; "coverage without power"; "degenerate case" | MC#failure-modes; MV#the-test-matrix; MS#example-the-order-intake-model |

## 3. Mechanism and justification

### 3.1 F1 — A pass is a comparison, not an event

The reference-case record is explicit: every verification case in the model contract has an identifier, a description, the expected result, the observed result, a pass/fail/not-run status and a test path. It then draws the line: "A case without a test path is not a verification case. A case marked pass without an observed result is a claim, not evidence." The model contract repeats the same structure — "verification: status, cases, observed result and test path" — and adds that "a verification case must name the test that exercised it."

This matters because "pass" is not a property of a process exit. It is the conclusion of a comparison between an expected boundary outcome and an observed one. A record that says "pass" because the run completed has the status word but not the comparison. The schema can require the fields, but the contract's own failure-mode list says what that buys: "Verification theater. A case is marked pass without a test path or an observed result. The strict schema rejects the missing fields; it cannot detect a false claim." The contract is "a guardrail, not a reviewer." So a schema-valid pass can still be theater if the observed result is merely "completed", if the expected result was copied from the run, or if no test path exists. The record in the question has the execution observation and the status word, but not the boundary observation that the status is supposed to summarize.

The book's own test matrix is also a summary, not the evidence record. It lists checks, test names and a result column, then says: "The table names the intended tests; the actual test file is tests/test_tycho_v12_engine.py. A test that is renamed must update the model contract's verification case path." The matrix's "pass" is navigation to the contract case; the contract case carries the observed result. A row that says "pass" without the case-level observed result is not the verification result.

### 3.2 F2 — Completion is not correctness

The run contract and the verification contract are different records. The run record contains model and scenario hashes, engine version, seed base, replications, metrics, convergence status, uncertainty, sensitivity, limitations and a result hash. It has no pass/fail verification status. Replay "proves that the stored inputs, engine version and seed produce the stored metrics on the same platform family"; it "is a reproducibility check, not a truth check." A completed, replayable run is therefore not a passed verification case.

The engine's life cycle writes the run record only after the model, scenario and result hashes are known, and a failed invariant aborts the run instead of writing a partial record. That is a real guarantee, but it is narrower than the boundary claim. The book's own conservation section says: "Conservation is necessary but not sufficient. A model can conserve requests while assigning them to the wrong outcome." A zero-server run can satisfy offered = completed + rejected + backlog and still be wrong if it puts requests in the wrong stock, fabricates completions, or mishandles the zero-capacity arithmetic. The engine's own failure-mode list includes "Partial write. A run record is written before an invariant check, leaving a plausible but invalid result." A plausible record is not a verified one.

The named failure mode is exactly the case in the question: "Asserting no exception. The test checks that the function returns, not that the result is correct." Completion establishes at most that the code path did not raise and that the checked invariants held. It does not establish the boundary outcome. That is why the record is not a verification result even if the engine is otherwise correct.

### 3.3 F3 — What the zero-server case must assert

The book gives the expected behavior directly: "zero servers: no service; requests are rejected or remain in backlog according to the model." The same section says a boundary case "often exposes a division by zero, a negative stock or an unbounded loop," and that "the tests assert the outcome, not merely that the run terminates." The Monte Carlo page adds: "The V12 tests assert the boundary outcome, not just that the run finishes."

For the stock-flow model, the arithmetic makes the expected outcome concrete. Service capacity is c times mu, and with c = 0 the capacity is zero, so served is zero and completed is zero. With positive arrivals and a bounded queue, admission fills the queue to its capacity and the excess is rejected; the backlog remains non-negative and bounded. With an unbounded queue, the backlog grows and the reported latency is "an artifact of the horizon" rather than a service property. The test must pin which configuration it is exercising: "rejected or remain in backlog according to the model" is a disjunction, and a disjunctive oracle cannot fail on the wrong branch. It must also handle the utilization formula lambda / (c * mu), whose denominator is zero at c = 0. A completion-only check would not detect an infinity, a NaN, a fabricated utilization or a silent default to one server; an outcome check must assert the explicit zero-capacity behavior.

The expected values must come from the model equations or a degenerate analytic answer, not from the current output. The reference-case overview says a reference case should have "an analytic answer, a clear tolerance and a failure mode that the test can detect." A test whose expected value is copied from the output is the named failure mode "Reference to a moving target. The expected value is copied from the current output, so the test can never fail." A zero-server case with exact zeros needs little tolerance, but it still needs an independently stated expectation and a comparison that can fail.

The case must also be non-vacuous. Zero arrivals and zero servers are listed as separate boundary cases. If zero servers are exercised only together with zero arrivals, no request ever reaches the server pool; a wrong service calculation still produces all zeros, so the case cannot distinguish "no service" from "no work". If the claim is about zero servers, offered load must be positive. This is an inference from the case definitions, not a claim that the current test does it; the distinction is what separates a boundary test from a smoke test that merely configures a degenerate file and runs it.

### 3.4 F4 — Boundary test vs. smoke test

A smoke test answers a narrow question: does the system start, load its inputs and return without an error? It is a liveness/wiring check. The V12 failure mode "Asserting no exception" describes exactly that pattern: "The test checks that the function returns, not that the result is correct." The book's V06 evaluation page makes the scope explicit for a different kind of smoke check: a 25/25 topic-routing smoke test "is not evidence of full-book search quality." The operations pattern makes the same distinction between process liveness, traffic readiness and functional behavior: the probes have "different failure meanings," and the choice should reverse when "application-specific logic, a dependency chain or functional behavior must be verified." A smoke test is allowed to be shallow; the error is treating its pass as a verification result.

A boundary test differs on five points:

1. Oracle: it has an independently specified expected outcome at the edge, not just "no exception."
2. Observation: it records the observed boundary values, not only the exit status.
3. Failure power: it can fail when the boundary behavior is wrong; a test that cannot fail is not verification.
4. Isolation: it actually exercises the boundary condition (positive offered load for zero servers), rather than combining it with another degenerate condition that masks it.
5. Traceability and scope: it has a case identifier, a test path, a pass/fail/not-run status and a stated model/configuration; it verifies one behavior at the edge, not the whole model.

A boundary test can contain a smoke precondition — run the path first, then assert the outcome — but the assertion is what makes it verification. The smoke part alone only says the system is wired up.

### 3.5 F5 — What even a genuine pass establishes

A passed zero-server case verifies the engine's implemented accounting at a degenerate point. It does not validate the model. The book states the distinction directly: "A model can be verified and still be invalid for a decision because its structure or data are wrong... A verified engine is not a validated system." Every V12 model is uncalibrated, and a validity limit is a condition on the result's use: the result holds only for the synthetic workload recorded in the scenario. The passing matrix covers only the exercised behaviors: "These are recorded as limits, not as completed checks. A reader who needs one of them must commission the corresponding evidence, not infer it from the passing matrix." Replay is a reproducibility check, not a truth check.

So the correct reading of even a well-formed zero-server pass is: the engine produced the specified zero-service behavior in the tested configuration. It is not evidence that the model is adequate for a decision, that its parameters are measured, that the queue discipline matches production, or that the system behaves this way outside the declared workload. The zero-server case is valuable precisely because it can catch division by zero, negative stock or an unbounded loop; it is not a validation of the model's structure or data.

### 3.6 F6 — How the record becomes theater

The record in the question fails at the first integrity check, but several distinct failures are worth separating:

- Verification theater: a pass without an observed result or a test path. The schema rejects missing fields; it cannot detect a false claim.
- Moving target: the expected value is copied from the current output, so the test can never fail.
- Happy-path-only: a model passes one steady-state run and fails at zero arrivals or full capacity; the boundary is where the model is weakest.
- Coverage without power: a case that cannot detect the error class adds coverage, not evidence. For zero servers, a completion-only check cannot detect fabricated service, a wrong rejection/backlog assignment, or a division-by-zero artifact.
- Combined degenerate case: zero arrivals plus zero servers is vacuous for the zero-server question, because no work is offered (inference from the separate case definitions).
- Matrix gap: the documented test matrix lists a zero-arrival boundary and a zero-queue-capacity boundary but no zero-server row, while the boundary-cases prose lists zero servers. The contract example records a below-capacity, a saturation and a zero-arrival boundary; it does not record a zero-server case. So the pages I read do not pair a zero-server case with a named test and observed result. A zero-server "pass" is not traceable in that matrix; it would need a case record with a test path and observed values to become a verification case. ## 4. Boundaries and trade-offs

Smoke tests are not worthless. They catch startup, import, schema-load and gross crash failures cheaply, and they can be a precondition for deeper tests. The mistake is calling their pass verification, not running them.

A boundary test can also be weak. A copied expected value, a disjunctive oracle, an undeclared tolerance, an observed result of "completed", or a test that cannot fail all produce a pass that is not evidence. The label "boundary" does not confer evidentiary power; the assertion does.

Zero-server behavior is model-dependent. "Rejected or remain in backlog according to the model" is not a single oracle. The test must pin the admission policy (bounded versus unbounded queue), the arrival rate, the queue capacity and the horizon. If it accepts either outcome, it cannot fail on the wrong one.

Non-vacuity is a design requirement. Zero arrivals plus zero servers cannot distinguish "no service" from "no work". If the claim is about zero servers, offered load must be positive; otherwise the case is a zero-arrival case with an unused configuration.

A schema-valid record is not proof. The strict schema rejects missing fields but cannot detect a false claim; an independent reviewer or a deliberately failing mutation is needed to show the case has power.

## 7. Bottom line

A zero-server run that merely completes is a smoke result: it shows the path executes, not that the engine produced the specified zero-service outcome. It becomes a verification result only when the record carries an independently stated expected boundary outcome, the observed values, a pass/fail judgement that can fail, and a test path — and even then it verifies the engine at a degenerate point, not the model's validity.

The tests assert the outcome, not merely that the run terminates.

A verification case record needs an identifier, a description, the expected result, the observed result, a pass, fail or not-run status, and a test path; a case without a test path is not a verification case.
A case marked pass without an observed result is a claim, not evidence.
